differences.what: the roof: a mansard, its steep lower face rising from the cornice to a curb about 7.4 m up with a low hipped deck above it, where the draft built a gable over two full storeys
differences.how: T-1936: r1 roof mansard, lower face 3.2 m (lower_m) over a 4.25 m eave; the deck the rules' 18-degree hip, its ridge about 8.9 m where the photograph reads about 9.2 m (within tolerance)

differences.what: the walls: ONE brick storey under the cornice (the cornice's top about 4.25 m over grade, read at x 1700 px), the second storey of the sheet's '2' being the mansard's; the draft stood two brick storeys to 6.2 m
differences.how: T-1936: r1 one storey of 4.25 m (storey_heights_m), the mansard its second

differences.how: T-1936: cornice 0.8 m deep, 0.4 m out (cornice_h_m, cornice_out_m); modillions every 1.2 m, 0.3 m tall, on all four faces; a 0.5 m stone course at 2.6 m (courses h_m)

differences.what: the barn's south end face, seen in the photograph from x 1893 to the edge: in the render the sheet's separate two-storey building south of the barn (r2: the 1911 sheet draws it in its own outline south of the barn's party wall) stands in front of it below about 7 m
differences.how: T-1936: the picture predates it. Neither the 1870s photograph nor the 1893 plate shows any building there (the barn's south face is seen whole from its cornice to its roof in the one, its corner in the other); the 1911 sheet draws it, so it was put up between 1893 and 1911, and the 1904 build stands it because the T-1841 census rules the sheet's building present_as_mapped in 1904 (a reconstruction, L-t1936-field-coach-house). The barn's south end is built behind it as the photograph shows it (cornice, brackets, frieze, mansard, one dormer, a stack).
